headline_result_summary: In a multi-level 2x2 factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial across Mumbai informal settlements (76 slums, 152 analyzed slum clusters, N = 6,652 households at 5-year endline), neither NGO-led bureaucratic facilitation (T1: helping household groups complete and submit online BMC water connection applications) nor bottom-up political coordination (T2: mobilizing collective petitions, delegations, and public pressure on elected officials) alone increased verified municipal piped water connections at endline (T1 main effect: +0.02, p = 0.26 in Full Sample; +0.04, one-sided p = 0.08 in Eligible Lands; T1 when T2=0: -0.04 and -0.03; T2 when T1=0: -0.08 and -0.06). In the full pre-registered sample—which includes 28 slums (36 clusters) on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands legally barred by court orders or municipal policy from receiving connections—even the combined T1*T2 interaction was statistically null (+0.11, SE = 0.08, p = 0.19 unadjusted; +0.05, SE = 0.07, p = 0.44 with covariates). However, in the pre-registered Eligible Lands subsample (48 slums, N = 5,251, where existing law/policy permitted formalization), bureaucratic assistance and political coordination showed strong positive complementarity: the T1*T2 interaction increased verified municipal water connections by +0.22 (SE = 0.10, two-sided p = 0.04; +0.20, SE = 0.08, p = 0.04 with covariates), and T1 conditional on T2 = 1 raised connection rates by +19 percentage points (p = 0.001, ~45% of the 0.42 control mean), driven primarily by settlements requiring multi-agency No Objection Certificates (+26 pp, p = 0.006) during the 2020-2022 pre-election period. At 1-year midline, T1 alone increased application submission (+10 pp, p < 0.01) and engineer visits (+4 pp, p < 0.01) without increasing connections, whereas on the pre-registered endline ordinal formalization scale (0-3) the T1*T2 interaction term itself was null (0.27, p = 0.28 Full; 0.34, p = 0.26 Eligible, though conditional marginal effect T1|T2=1 in Eligible Lands was +0.39, p = 0.046).
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Full Sample vs. Eligible Lands Subsample: Seven of the eight primary pre-registered regression tests across Table 1 (Cols 1-3) and Table S18 (Cols 1-4) are statistically non-significant at p < 0.05. The headline positive complementarity effect on binary Formalized appears only in the Eligible Lands subsample (Table 1 Col 4: T1*T2 = 0.22, p = 0.04; AME of T1|T2=1 = +0.19, p = 0.001), which excludes 28 slums on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands via a July 2019 PAP amendment; in the full 76-slum sample, T1*T2 is null (0.11, p = 0.19 unadjusted; 0.05, p = 0.44 adjusted). 2. Single-arm vs. joint treatment coding: Coding T1 (bureaucratic assistance) or T2 (political mobilization) in isolation yields null effects on endline water connections (and slightly negative non-significant lower-order coefficients, -0.02 to -0.08, when the other arm is 0); positive connection gains require both T1 and T2 together in policy-eligible slums. 3. Raw unclustered means vs. clustered WLS: Appendix Figure S1 (PDF p. 56) displays a raw unclustered p = 0.00 negative difference for 'Just T2' vs. Control in the Full Sample, which disappears once block fixed effects, slum-level weighting, and slum-clustered standard errors are applied (Table 1 Col 2: -0.08, SE = 0.06). 4. Binary Formalized vs. Ordinal Formalization Level: On the pre-registered 0-3 ordinal scale (Table S18), the T1*T2 interaction term is statistically null in both samples (p = 0.28 and p = 0.26), even though the conditional marginal effect of T1 when T2 = 1 in Eligible Lands reaches +0.39 (p = 0.046). 5. Test-sidedness: T1 main-effect p-values in Table 1 Cols 1 & 3 (p = 0.26, p = 0.08) are one-sided, whereas interaction p-values in Cols 2 & 4 (p = 0.19, p = 0.04) are two-sided.
study_design: Multi-level 2x2 factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial (field experiment) with block-randomization of 76 slums to Political Coordination (T2) and complete randomization of 152 slum clusters within slums to Bureaucratic Assistance (T1), evaluated via weighted least squares (WLS) regressions with randomization block fixed effects and clustered standard errors at 1-year midline (2019) and 5-year endline (2023).
unit_and_sample_size: Households nested within slum clusters (152 analyzed of 153 mapped clusters of 50-200 households) and slums (76 slums in Full Sample; 48 slums / 116 clusters in Eligible Lands Sample after excluding 28 slums / 36 clusters on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands). Endline analytic N = 6,652 households in Full Sample (including 61.5% recontacted baseline respondents plus 2,444 replacement-sample households) and N = 5,251 households in Eligible Lands Sample; Midline analytic N = 6,268 (Full Sample) and N = 5,010 (Eligible Lands Sample).
